opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the epidemiology was the easy part. In February 2020 you could look at the exponential curves, the case counts in Wuhan and northern Italy, and the doubling times, and the conclusion was just arithmetic. It was going to sweep the world, and a lot of very smart, credentialed people were still saying "it's just the flu" or "don't panic." I bet on that, and that part played out.

What I underestimated was the societal response, in both directions.

First, I underestimated how dysfunctional some of the institutions would be. I didn't expect the CDC to botch testing so badly, or the mask guidance to flip-flop, or the FDA to be such a bottleneck at the moment speed mattered most. You assume the people whose job it is to handle this have a plan. Often they didn't.

Second, and more interesting to me, I underestimated how big the response would be once it finally came. Everyone was asleep, and then within a few weeks the whole world flipped. Entire economies shut down. Congress passed trillions of dollars in spending almost overnight, things that would have seemed politically impossible a month earlier. Operation Warp Speed got vaccines out in under a year. Once the threat became undeniable and visceral, the Overton window didn't shift gradually. It just snapped.

That's the lesson I carry over to AI. People look at the current political discourse and assume it'll stay that way: a niche issue, some think tanks, a few hearings. But I think there's going to be a similar moment where it becomes undeniable, and then the response will be far more dramatic than people expect. The question is whether we've done the thinking in advance, so that when the window snaps open, we actually do the right things rather than flailing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he underestimated the societal response and specifically how large it became, describing shutdowns, trillions in spending, and rapid vaccine development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I most underestimated wasn't the virus. The virus I basically got right. By late January, early February you could look at the Wuhan numbers, look at the doubling time, look at the fact that it was already in Italy and Iran, and the exponential just did what exponentials do. That part felt almost mechanical.

What I underestimated was how slow the institutions would be. I had this naive model where I assumed that once the information was out there, once the New York Times was running the stories and the preprints were piling up, the people whose actual job it was to respond would respond. The CDC, the FDA, the WHO, the universities, the big companies. I figured I was just early, and that being early meant maybe a two week head start on everyone else. Instead it turned out that being early meant you were early by months, because most of the system wasn't going to move until it was physically forced to.

And I think the deeper mistake was about how people update. I assumed that smart people with good information update smoothly. They don't. They sit on a prior for a very long time, and then they panic all at once. So in February it was "this is just the flu," and then in mid-March, in the space of about ten days, everyone flipped to full lockdown. There was almost no intermediate state where the response was proportional to the evidence. That whiplash, the fact that the world goes from zero to a hundred rather than tracking the curve, that's what surprised me.

The other thing, which I think about a lot now in the AI context, is that I underestimated how little the forecast itself mattered. Being right in February bought you basically nothing unless you had already done the work of putting yourself in a position to act on it. A handful of people made real decisions, shorted the market, stocked up, moved out of cities. Most people who saw it coming, including a lot of my friends, just sort of watched it happen with a kind of frustrated omniscience. That taught me that the question isn't "can you see it coming," it's "who is in the room when the decisions get made, and have they been prepared in advance." That's a lesson I've tried to carry over to everything since.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the response shifted from dismissing COVID-19 to full lockdown in about ten days, describing the societal reaction as a surprising “zero to a hundred” whiplash.

astra-6.text:
I think I underestimated how hard it is to translate seeing something coming into knowing what to do about it. You can look at exponential growth and say, “This is going to spread around the world.” But that doesn’t tell you how people will respond, what institutions will do, or what your own life will look like six months later.

There’s also a difference between intellectually believing something and actually internalizing it. You can think a pandemic is coming and still have all these plans that implicitly assume normal life will continue. The prediction can change much faster than the rest of your mental model.

r001.rationale: The response says he failed to anticipate how people and institutions would respond, but it does not identify the magnitude of society’s reaction as the specific thing he underestimated.

sol-6.1.text:
I underestimated how hard it would be to turn that prediction into good decisions. You could look at exponential growth and conclude that this was going to become a pandemic. But that didn’t automatically tell you how governments would respond, how people would change their behavior, or what the economic consequences would be.

There’s a big gap between seeing the broad outline of something coming and understanding how it will actually unfold. You can be ahead of the curve on the central prediction and still be surprised by much of what follows.

r001.rationale: The response mentions government responses and changes in people’s behavior, but it identifies uncertainty about how events would unfold—not the magnitude of society’s reaction—as the thing Aschenbrenner underestimated.
